items.stem: Which is the definition of tensile stress?
items.answer: Force per unit cross-sectional area
items.markingKey: σ = F/A.

items.stem: Explain why the Young modulus is a property of a material but the spring constant is a property of a particular sample.
items.answer: E = stress/strain does not depend on the dimensions of the sample; k = F/x depends on the length and cross-sectional area as well as the material (k = EA/L).
items.markingKey: E independent of dimensions [1]; k depends on L and A [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how to measure the Young modulus of a metal wire in the laboratory.
items.answer: Clamp a long thin wire; measure L with a metre rule and d at several places with a micrometer; add loads and measure extension with a vernier/marker against a reference wire; plot stress against strain; E = gradient of the linear region.
items.markingKey: long wire and measurement of L [1]; micrometer for d [1]; extension measured as load added [1]; E from gradient of stress-strain [1] [4]

items.stem: A brass wire of length 2.5 m and diameter 0.50 mm supports a load of 50 N. The Young modulus of brass is 1.0 × 10¹¹ Pa. Calculate the stress in the wire.
A tungsten wire of length 1.5 m and diameter 0.50 mm supports a load of 50 N. The Young modulus of tungsten is 4.1 × 10¹¹ Pa. Calculate the extension of the wire.

In a school laboratory in Colombo, a student hangs loads on a copper wire of length 2.5 m and diameter 0.40 mm to find its Young modulus. (a) Define stress and strain. (b) Suggest why a reference wire with a vernier scale is used to measure the extension.
items.answer: (a) stress = force/cross-sectional area; strain = extension/original length (b) It compensates for sagging of the support and temperature changes; the vernier measures small extensions precisely.
items.markingKey: (a) stress [1]; strain [1] [2] (b) compensates sag/temperature [1]; precise small extension [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the definition of tensile strain?
items.answer: Extension divided by original length
items.markingKey: ε = x/L, no unit.

items.stem: What is the unit of the Young modulus?
items.answer: Pa
items.markingKey: Stress (Pa) ÷ strain (no unit).

items.stem: Explain why a long, thin wire is used to measure the Young modulus.
items.answer: A long wire gives a larger extension (x ∝ L) and a thin wire gives a large stress for a given load, so the extension is large enough to measure with small percentage uncertainty.
items.markingKey: long → larger extension [1]; thin → larger stress/extension [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the diameter of the wire should be measured at several points along its length.
items.answer: The wire may not be uniform; averaging several readings (at different orientations) gives a more reliable value for the area, and d is squared in A so its uncertainty matters.
items.markingKey: non-uniform wire [1]; average reduces uncertainty, which is doubled in A [1] [2]

items.stem: A steel cable supports a load within its limit of proportionality. The cross-sectional area is multiplied by 4 while the load and original length stay the same. Explain how the extension changes.
items.answer: The extension becomes a quarter.
items.markingKey: Using x = FL/(EA): extension ∝ cross-sectional area^-1.00; factor = 4.00^-1.00 = 0.250. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A copper wire is stretched in a Young modulus experiment, within the elastic limit. The original length is multiplied by 5 while the load and cross-sectional area stay the same. Explain how the extension changes.
items.answer: The extension becomes 5 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using x = FL/(EA): extension ∝ original length; factor = 5.00 = 5.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A nylon wire has cross-sectional area 2.83 × 10⁻⁷ m² and supports a load of 50 N. What is the tensile stress?
Wire P and wire Q are made of brass. Q has 3 times the diameter of P and twice the length. The same load is hung on each. Determine the ratio extension of Q / extension of P.
A aluminium wire of length 3.0 m and diameter 0.40 mm supports a load of 100 N. The Young modulus of aluminium is 7.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa. Calculate the stress in the wire.
A tungsten wire of length 2.0 m and diameter 0.40 mm supports a load of 40 N. The Young modulus of tungsten is 4.1 × 10¹¹ Pa. Calculate the stress in the wire.
A nylon wire of length 3.0 m and diameter 0.40 mm supports a load of 120 N. The Young modulus of nylon is 3.0 × 10⁹ Pa. Calculate the extension of the wire.
items.answer: 955 mm

items.stem: A wire of length 2.0 m and diameter 0.60 mm extends by 1.38 mm when a load of 80 N is added. (a) Calculate the stress and the strain. (b) Calculate the Young modulus and suggest the material, using: steel 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa, copper 1.2 × 10¹¹ Pa, brass 1.0 × 10¹¹ Pa, aluminium 7.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa, nylon 3.0 × 10⁹ Pa, tungsten 4.1 × 10¹¹ Pa.
items.answer: (a) σ = 2.83 × 10⁸ Pa, ε = 6.90 × 10⁻⁴ (b) E = 4.10 × 10¹¹ Pa: tungsten

items.stem: A copper wire 2.5 m long with diameter 0.50 mm is fixed to a ceiling beam and loaded with masses. (a) With a load of 60 N the extension is 6.37 mm. Calculate the Young modulus. (b) State one safety precaution for this experiment.
items.answer: (a) 1.20 × 10¹¹ Pa (b) Wear safety goggles in case the wire snaps / place a box of sand under the masses.
items.markingKey: (a) σ/ε (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 1.20 × 10¹¹ Pa [1] [3] (b) Wear safety goggles in case the wire snaps / place a box of sand under the masses [1]

items.stem: A brass wire 2.0 m long with diameter 0.50 mm is fixed to a ceiling beam and loaded with masses. (a) Define stress and strain. (b) With a load of 100 N the extension is 10.2 mm. Calculate the Young modulus.
items.answer: (a) stress = force/cross-sectional area; strain = extension/original length (b) 1.00 × 10¹¹ Pa
items.markingKey: (a) stress [1]; strain [1] [2] (b) σ/ε (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 1.00 × 10¹¹ Pa [1] [3]

items.stem: What is meant by elastic deformation?
options: Deformation from which the material returns to its original shape when the load is removed
Deformation that only occurs in rubber
Deformation in which the material breaks
items.answer: Deformation from which the material returns to its original shape when the load is removed
items.markingKey: Elastic: fully recoverable.

items.stem: Describe the force-extension graph for a ductile metal such as copper, loaded until it breaks.
items.answer: Straight line through the origin (Hooke's law) to the limit of proportionality; then curves past the elastic limit; large plastic extension with little extra force (necking) until fracture.
items.markingKey: linear region [1]; elastic limit then plastic region with large extension [1]; breaks after necking [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a brittle and a ductile material, giving an example of each.
items.answer: A brittle material (e.g. glass) breaks with little or no plastic deformation; a ductile material (e.g. copper) undergoes large plastic deformation before breaking and can be drawn into wires.
items.markingKey: brittle: no plastic deformation, example [1]; ductile: large plastic deformation, example [1] [2]

items.stem: A spring of spring constant 80 N m⁻¹ obeys Hooke's law. Determine the extension produced by a load of 2.0 N, in cm.
items.answer: 2.5 cm
items.markingKey: x = F/k = 2.0/80 m = 2.5 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Two identical springs, each of spring constant 100 N m⁻¹, are connected in parallel. A load of 8.0 N hangs from the combination. Calculate the total extension.
items.answer: 4.0 cm

items.stem: Engineers compare the force-extension behaviour of a steel cable, a rubber mounting and a ceramic rod. (a) Distinguish between elastic and plastic deformation. (b) Describe the behaviour of the brittle material. (c) State Hooke's law.
items.answer: (a) Elastic: returns to original shape when load removed; plastic: permanent change in shape. (b) Linear up to fracture with no plastic region. (c) Extension is proportional to load provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
items.markingKey: (a) elastic [1]; plastic [1] [2] (b) Linear up to fracture with no plastic region [1] (c) Extension is proportional to load provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded [1]

items.stem: What is meant by plastic deformation?
options: Permanent deformation that remains when the load is removed
items.answer: Permanent deformation that remains when the load is removed
items.markingKey: Plastic: beyond the elastic limit.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State what is meant by the elastic limit. (b) What is meant by elastic deformation?
items.answer: (a) The maximum load (or stress) beyond which the material will not return to its original length when the load is removed. (b) Deformation from which the material returns to its original shape when the load is removed
items.markingKey: (a) beyond it deformation is permanent [1] (b) Elastic: fully recoverable.

items.stem: Explain how you could show that a spring has been loaded beyond its elastic limit.
items.answer: Remove the load and measure the length; if it does not return to its original length there is a permanent extension, so the elastic limit was exceeded.
items.markingKey: unload and measure length [1]; permanent extension shows limit exceeded [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the loading and unloading curves for a rubber band.
items.answer: Non-linear loading curve; the unloading curve lies below it (hysteresis) but returns to near zero extension; the area between the curves is energy converted to thermal energy.
items.markingKey: non-linear [1]; unloading below loading [1]; area = energy dissipated [1] [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how you could show that a spring has been loaded beyond its elastic limit. (b) Explain the difference between a brittle and a ductile material, giving an example of each.

items.answer: 20 cm

items.answer: (a) 50 N m⁻¹ (b) about 5 N (c) remove the loads and check whether the spring returns to its original length.

items.stem: A spring of spring constant 25 N m⁻¹ is connected in series with a spring of spring constant 120 N m⁻¹. A load of 4.0 N hangs from the lower spring. (a) Calculate the extension of each spring. (b) Calculate the spring constant of the combination. (c) State the assumption made.

items.stem: A student in an AS Physics lesson in Doha investigates samples of copper wire, glass fibre and rubber by loading them and measuring extension. (a) Sketch and describe the force-extension graph for the ductile metal. (b) Describe the behaviour of the brittle material.

items.stem: Engineers compare the force-extension behaviour of a steel cable, a rubber mounting and a ceramic rod. (a) Describe the behaviour of the brittle material. (b) Explain what the area between the loading and unloading curves for rubber represents. (c) State Hooke's law.

items.stem: The elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire is represented by …
options: the gradient of the force-extension graph
the area under the force-extension graph
the area under the stress-strain graph multiplied by the mass
items.answer: the area under the force-extension graph
items.markingKey: Work done stretching = ∫F dx.

items.stem: Derive E = ½Fx for a material that obeys Hooke's law.
items.answer: The force rises linearly from 0 to F as the extension goes from 0 to x; the work done is the area of the triangle under the graph, ½Fx.
items.markingKey: work = area under graph [1]; triangle area ½Fx [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the energy released when a wire stretched beyond its elastic limit is unloaded is less than the work done in stretching it.
items.answer: Some of the work done causes plastic deformation and is transferred to thermal energy; only the elastic part is recovered.
items.markingKey: plastic deformation [1]; energy dissipated as thermal, not recovered [1] [2]

items.stem: A trampoline spring with k = 800 N m⁻¹ is extended by 10 cm, within the limit of proportionality. Determine the elastic potential energy stored.
items.markingKey: E = ½kx² = ½ × 800 × 0.10² = 4.0 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A trampoline spring with k = 50 N m⁻¹ is extended by 2.0 cm and used to launch a ball of mass 0.010 kg horizontally. Assuming all the elastic energy becomes kinetic energy, calculate the launch speed.

items.markingKey: x = F/k = 4.0/25 m = 16 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A student loads a spring and records the extension: 1 N: 2.0 cm, 2 N: 4.0 cm, 3 N: 6.0 cm, 4 N: 8.0 cm, 5 N: 12.5 cm, 6 N: 18.0 cm. (a) Determine the spring constant from the linear region. (b) Estimate the load at the limit of proportionality. (c) Explain how the student could check whether the elastic limit was exceeded.
items.answer: (a) 50 N m⁻¹ (b) about 4 N (c) remove the loads and check whether the spring returns to its original length.
items.markingKey: (a) k = F/x from linear region = 50 N m⁻¹ [1] (b) 4 N where proportionality ends [1] (c) unload and measure length [1] [3]

items.stem: Engineers compare the force-extension behaviour of a steel cable, a rubber mounting and a ceramic rod. (a) Sketch and describe the force-extension graph for the ductile metal. (b) Describe the behaviour of the brittle material. (c) State Hooke's law.
items.answer: (a) Linear to limit of proportionality, then curve with large plastic extension before breaking. (b) Linear up to fracture with no plastic region. (c) Extension is proportional to load provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
items.markingKey: (a) linear region [1]; plastic region and fracture [1] [2] (b) Linear up to fracture with no plastic region [1] (c) Extension is proportional to load provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded [1]

items.stem: Engineers compare the force-extension behaviour of a steel cable, a rubber mounting and a ceramic rod. (a) Distinguish between elastic and plastic deformation. (b) Describe the behaviour of the brittle material. (c) Explain what the area between the loading and unloading curves for rubber represents. (d) State Hooke's law.
items.answer: (a) Elastic: returns to original shape when load removed; plastic: permanent change in shape. (b) Linear up to fracture with no plastic region. (c) Energy transferred to thermal energy (hysteresis) in each cycle. (d) Extension is proportional to load provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
items.markingKey: (a) elastic [1]; plastic [1] [2] (b) Linear up to fracture with no plastic region [1] (c) energy lost per loading cycle [1]; transferred to thermal energy (hysteresis) [1] [2] (d) Extension is proportional to load provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A spring of spring constant 200 N m⁻¹ is stretched by 0.10 m. What elastic potential energy is stored? (b) The extension of a spring is doubled within its limit of proportionality. The elastic potential energy …
items.answer: (a) 1.0 J (b) is multiplied by 4

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Derive E = ½Fx for a material that obeys Hooke's law. (b) Explain why the energy released when a wire stretched beyond its elastic limit is unloaded is less than the work done in stretching it.
items.answer: (a) The force rises linearly from 0 to F as the extension goes from 0 to x; the work done is the area of the triangle under the graph, ½Fx. (b) Some of the work done causes plastic deformation and is transferred to thermal energy; only the elastic part is recovered.
items.markingKey: (a) work = area under graph [1]; triangle area ½Fx [1] [2] (b) plastic deformation [1]; energy dissipated as thermal, not recovered [1] [2]

items.stem: The force-extension graph for a metal wire is a straight line from the origin to (4.0 mm, 40 N) and then a straight line to (7.0 mm, 50 N). Calculate the work done in stretching the wire to an extension of 7.0 mm.

A catapult band behaves like a spring of constant 50 N m⁻¹ and is stretched by 8.0 cm and used to launch a ball of mass 0.010 kg horizontally. Assuming all the elastic energy becomes kinetic energy, calculate the launch speed.

A buffer spring at the end of a model railway in Cape Town has k = 500 N m⁻¹. A 0.50 kg truck compresses it by 5.0 cm before stopping. (a) Calculate the maximum force exerted by the spring. (b) Explain why the elastic potential energy is the area under the force-compression graph. (c) State one assumption made in your calculation.
items.answer: (a) 25 N (b) Work done = force × displacement; the force varies, so the work is the area under the graph. (c) The spring obeys Hooke's law / no energy lost to friction or heat.

items.stem: A force of 200 N acts on a wire of cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m². What is the stress?
Answer both parts. (a) Describe how to measure the Young modulus of a metal wire in the laboratory. (b) Explain why the diameter of the wire should be measured at several points along its length.
items.answer: (a) Clamp a long thin wire; measure L with a metre rule and d at several places with a micrometer; add loads and measure extension with a vernier/marker against a reference wire; plot stress against strain; E = gradient of the linear region. (b) The wire may not be uniform; averaging several readings (at different orientations) gives a more reliable value for the area, and d is squared in A so its uncertainty matters.
items.markingKey: (a) long wire and measurement of L [1]; micrometer for d [1]; extension measured as load added [1]; E from gradient of stress-strain [1] [4] (b) non-uniform wire [1]; average reduces uncertainty, which is doubled in A [1] [2]

items.stem: A steel cable supports a load within its limit of proportionality. The original length is doubled while the load and cross-sectional area stay the same. Predict, with a reason, how the extension changes.
items.answer: The extension doubles.
items.markingKey: Using x = FL/(EA): extension ∝ original length; factor = 2.00 = 2.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

A brass wire 2.0 m long with diameter 0.50 mm is fixed to a ceiling beam and loaded with masses. (a) Define stress and strain. (b) Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire. (c) Suggest why a reference wire with a vernier scale is used to measure the extension.
items.answer: (a) stress = force/cross-sectional area; strain = extension/original length (b) 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m² (c) It compensates for sagging of the support and temperature changes; the vernier measures small extensions precisely.

items.answer: 50 N m⁻¹

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe the force-extension graph for a ductile metal such as copper, loaded until it breaks. (b) Explain how you could show that a spring has been loaded beyond its elastic limit.
items.answer: (a) Straight line through the origin (Hooke's law) to the limit of proportionality; then curves past the elastic limit; large plastic extension with little extra force (necking) until fracture. (b) Remove the load and measure the length; if it does not return to its original length there is a permanent extension, so the elastic limit was exceeded.
items.markingKey: (a) linear region [1]; elastic limit then plastic region with large extension [1]; breaks after necking [1] [3] (b) unload and measure length [1]; permanent extension shows limit exceeded [1] [2]
